concepts.title: Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Rolling Updates
concepts.description: A Deployment never runs Pods directly. It manages a ReplicaSet, which manages Pods, and this layering of two separate controllers is what makes zero-downtime rolling updates and instant rollbacks possible without you writing any orchestration logic.
learningObjectives: Explain the layered relationship Deployment -> ReplicaSet -> Pod and what each layer is specifically responsible for.
Explain why Deployments create a new ReplicaSet on every change to the Pod template, rather than mutating the existing one in place.
Describe the default rolling update strategy (maxSurge/maxUnavailable) and explain what problem it solves compared to deleting all old Pods before creating new ones.
Use kubectl rollout status/history/undo to inspect and control a rollout.
Predict how a rolling update behaves when the new Pod template is broken (crash-looping or failing readiness), and explain why the rollout stalls rather than completing.
Explain why manually deleting a Pod owned by a Deployment doesn't reduce the total running count.

sections.heading: Three Layers, Three Distinct Jobs
sections.body:
A **Deployment** is the object you write and edit. It remembers the *desired Pod template*, the *desired replica count*, and the *update strategy*, and it never creates or touches a Pod itself. Its job is versioning the Pod template over time and orchestrating a safe transition whenever that template changes.

A **ReplicaSet** is what the Deployment manages, and its job is much narrower: given a fixed Pod template and a selector, make sure N Pods matching that selector exist, at all times. A ReplicaSet has no concept of 'update,' 'version,' or 'rollback'; it is a count enforcer. That has a surprising consequence: if you edit a live ReplicaSet's Pod template directly, none of its *already-running* Pods change. The edit only affects Pods the ReplicaSet creates from then on, because a ReplicaSet reconciles count, not content, against its existing Pods.

A **Pod** is the running unit, as covered in the previous module. You can see the three-layer chain in the generated names: a Deployment named `web` produces a ReplicaSet named something like `web-7d9f8c9b7` (the suffix is a hash of the Pod template), which produces Pods named `web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp`. The hash isn't cosmetic: it's how the Deployment controller tells 'I already have a ReplicaSet for this template' from 'this is a new template that needs a new ReplicaSet.'

sections.heading: Why a New ReplicaSet Per Change, Not an Edited One
sections.body:
When you change `.spec.template` on a Deployment (bumping an image tag is the everyday case), the Deployment controller computes a hash of the new Pod template. If a ReplicaSet with that hash already exists (this happens on a rollback, covered below), it reuses it; otherwise it creates a new ReplicaSet, initially scaled to 0, and begins shifting replica counts between the old and new ReplicaSets at a pace dictated by the rolling update strategy: scale the new one up, scale the old one down, repeat, until the new one holds the full desired count and the old one holds zero.

Old ReplicaSets are not deleted once they reach zero replicas. They're retained as scaled-to-zero objects, up to a configurable `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10). That is what makes `kubectl rollout undo` fast and reliable: a rollback isn't a rebuild, it's 'scale the previous ReplicaSet back up, scale the current one back down,' the same mechanism as a forward rollout pointed at an existing ReplicaSet instead of a new one.

This also explains why editing a running ReplicaSet's Pod template directly is pointless for anything you want to persist. Existing Pods are untouched, and the Deployment controller doesn't adopt the mutated template as its desired state, so the next Deployment-driven change will most likely create yet another new ReplicaSet from the Deployment's own unedited template and sideline your edit.

sections.heading: Rolling Updates: maxSurge and maxUnavailable
sections.body:
The default Deployment strategy is `RollingUpdate`, governed by two knobs: `maxSurge` (how many Pods above the desired count may exist temporarily) and `maxUnavailable` (how many Pods below the desired count are tolerated temporarily). Both default to 25%, with maxSurge rounded up and maxUnavailable rounded down (for 4 replicas, 25% is exactly 1 each; for 3 replicas, maxSurge becomes 1 and maxUnavailable 0).

Take 4 desired replicas with `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`. The controller may briefly go up to 5 total Pods, and available Pods never drop below 4. It creates 1 new Pod, waits for it to become Ready, then deletes 1 old Pod, and repeats until the new ReplicaSet holds all 4 and the old one holds 0. The number of available Pods never hits zero, which is what makes a rollout 'zero downtime.' This isn't traffic-draining magic; it's gated on the new Pod's **readiness probe** reporting healthy. If a new Pod starts but never becomes Ready, the rollout stalls there instead of replacing everything with broken Pods, because each step waits on readiness. A nonzero `maxUnavailable` loosens this: with `maxUnavailable: 1` the controller may delete an old Pod right away, without waiting for the new one to become Ready, as long as at least 3 stay available.

```yaml
spec:
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
```

Compare the `Recreate` strategy, which deletes *all* old Pods first and only then creates the new ones. That is a real downtime window, appropriate only for workloads that cannot run two versions at once (an exclusive lock on a shared resource, an in-place schema migration that both versions can't safely straddle).

sections.heading: Watching, Pausing, and Undoing a Rollout
sections.body:
`kubectl rollout status deployment/web` blocks and streams progress until the rollout completes or times out. It's the most useful command for verifying a rollout finished instead of assuming so because `apply` returned instantly. `kubectl rollout history deployment/web` lists prior revisions, each mapped to a ReplicaSet. `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` uses the mechanism from the previous section: scale the previous revision's ReplicaSet back up and the current one down. Rollbacks are typically fast because no new Pod template has to be computed and, if the node still has the older image cached, nothing needs pulling. `kubectl rollout pause` and `kubectl rollout resume` let you halt a rollout partway through, which is useful for a manual canary-style check before committing to the rest. `kubectl rollout history deployment/web --revision=2` shows the Pod template of one revision, and `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=2` rolls back to that specific revision instead of just the previous one.

One more field to know: `progressDeadlineSeconds`. If a rollout hasn't made progress within this window (default 600s), the Deployment sets a `ProgressDeadlineExceeded` condition in `.status.conditions`, visible via `kubectl describe deployment`. That is what lets a CI/CD pipeline running `kubectl rollout status` fail fast on a broken rollout instead of hanging while it waits for Pods that will never become Ready.

sections.heading: Desired Replicas Is Enforced, Even Against You
sections.body:
A common early surprise: you `kubectl delete pod web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp` expecting one fewer running Pod, and a few seconds later `kubectl get pods` shows the same total, with one Pod's name and IP changed. The ReplicaSet controller saw the actual count drop below the desired count and created a replacement. Deleting a Pod doesn't say 'I want one fewer.' The only way to change the desired count is to change `.spec.replicas` on the Deployment (or ReplicaSet); to the controller, deleting a Pod it owns looks the same as that Pod crashing.

Underneath is `ownerReferences`: every Pod created by a ReplicaSet carries an entry pointing back to that ReplicaSet's UID. That's how the controller knows which Pods are its own to count, and how cascading deletion works: deleting a Deployment cascades by default to its ReplicaSets, which cascade to their Pods, all driven by the owner-reference chain with no special-cased deletion logic. `kubectl delete deployment web --cascade=orphan` breaks the chain on purpose: it removes only the Deployment and leaves its ReplicaSets and Pods running.

examples.title: Seeing the Three-Layer Chain and Its Naming Pattern
examples.code:
kubectl get deployment web
# NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
# web    3/3     3            3

kubectl get rs -l app=web
# NAME               DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
# web-7d9f8c9b7       3         3         3

kubectl get pods -l app=web
# NAME                     READY   STATUS
# web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp      1/1     Running
# web-7d9f8c9b7-9plm2      1/1     Running
# web-7d9f8c9b7-k7q3z      1/1     Running
examples.explanation: The ReplicaSet's name, web-7d9f8c9b7, carries the same hash that starts every Pod name it owns. The hash is computed from the Pod template, and it's how the Deployment controller recognizes 'this ReplicaSet corresponds to this template' when deciding whether to reuse an existing ReplicaSet or create a new one on the next template change. `kubectl get pod web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}'` would print `web-7d9f8c9b7`: the Pod's recorded owner is the ReplicaSet, not the Deployment `web`, which is the layering this concept is about.

examples.title: A maxSurge/maxUnavailable Rollout, Step by Step
examples.code:
Deployment: replicas=4, maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0
Rolling from ReplicaSet-OLD (image v1) to ReplicaSet-NEW (image v2)

Step 0 (start):   OLD=4  NEW=0   total=4  available=4
Step 1 (surge):   OLD=4  NEW=1   total=5  available=4  (waiting for 1 NEW pod to become Ready)
Step 2 (shrink):  OLD=3  NEW=1   total=4  available=4  (1 OLD pod deleted once NEW pod was Ready)
Step 3 (surge):   OLD=3  NEW=2   total=5  available=4
Step 4 (shrink):  OLD=2  NEW=2   total=4  available=4
Step 5 (surge):   OLD=2  NEW=3   total=5  available=4
Step 6 (shrink):  OLD=1  NEW=3   total=4  available=4
Step 7 (surge):   OLD=1  NEW=4   total=5  available=4
Step 8 (shrink):  OLD=0  NEW=4   total=4  available=4  (rollout complete)
examples.explanation: The 'available' column never drops below 4 (the desired count) and 'total' never exceeds 5, the bounds that maxUnavailable=0 and maxSurge=1 set: never short of desired, never more than 1 over. Each shrink step (deleting an OLD pod) happens only after the preceding surge step's NEW pod is confirmed Ready. If that NEW pod's readiness probe never passes, the sequence freezes at whichever surge step it's on rather than deleting more OLD pods and driving available capacity down. That is why a correct readinessProbe on the new Pod template matters so much to the zero-downtime guarantee: without one (or with one that always reports ready), the controller has no reliable signal to gate on. With maxUnavailable=1 instead, the controller could delete an OLD pod at step 1 without waiting, and 'available' would dip to 3.

examples.title: A Broken Rollout, Stalled, Then Rolled Back
examples.code:
kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:typo-tag
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
# Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 2 out of 4 new replicas have been updated...
# (hangs here: the new Pods can't pull nginx:typo-tag, so they never become Ready)

# In another terminal:
kubectl get pods -l app=web
# web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp    1/1   Running            (OLD, still serving traffic)
# web-7d9f8c9b7-9plm2    1/1   Running            (OLD, still serving traffic)
# web-7d9f8c9b7-k7q3z    1/1   Running            (OLD, still serving traffic)
# web-8a1e2f4c3-h9z1x    0/1   ImagePullBackOff   (NEW, stuck)
# web-8a1e2f4c3-p5d2w    0/1   ImagePullBackOff   (NEW, stuck)

kubectl rollout undo deployment/web
# deployment.apps/web rolled back
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
# deployment "web" successfully rolled out
examples.explanation: With the default 25% settings and 4 replicas, maxSurge works out to 1 (rounded up) and maxUnavailable to 1 (rounded down). The controller created one new Pod, was then allowed to remove one old Pod right away (availability may fall to 3), created a second new Pod, and ran out of budget: both new Pods are stuck pulling a tag that doesn't exist, and removing another old Pod would drop availability below 3. The rollout froze with 3 healthy old Pods still serving traffic. This is the payoff of gating on readiness: a bad image never gets to replace every healthy Pod. `kubectl rollout undo` then triggers the same scale-up/scale-down mechanism as a forward rollout, pointed at the previous (still-retained) ReplicaSet, which is why it resolves quickly: no new template hashing, no pull of a fresh version, just re-balancing replica counts between two ReplicaSets that already exist. To see why the new Pods are stuck, run `kubectl describe pod` on one of them: the Events section shows the failed image pull.

misconceptions.description: Deployments manage Pods directly -- the Deployment object is the 'owner' of the Pods it creates.
misconceptions.clarification: The ownership chain is Deployment -> ReplicaSet -> Pod, and a Pod's ownerReferences entry points to the ReplicaSet, never to the Deployment. You can confirm it: `kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml` shows ownerReferences with kind: ReplicaSet. This isn't pedantry. During a rollout you will see two ReplicaSets owning nonzero counts of Pods for the same Deployment, which only makes sense once you know the Deployment never owned any Pod; it only owns ReplicaSets.
misconceptions.fact: The ownership chain is Deployment -> ReplicaSet -> Pod, and a Pod's ownerReferences entry points to the ReplicaSet, never to the Deployment.

misconceptions.description: Editing a running ReplicaSet's Pod template YAML directly, or deleting individual Pods it owns, is a normal way to push out a new version of an application.
misconceptions.clarification: A ReplicaSet has no update or versioning logic: editing its template only affects Pods it creates after the edit, and every already-running Pod is left alone. And if that ReplicaSet is owned by a Deployment, the Deployment controller doesn't treat your mutated template as its desired state, so the next Deployment-driven change is likely to sideline your edit or create a separate new ReplicaSet alongside it. The supported way to ship a new version is to change the Deployment's own .spec.template, which triggers the create-a-new-ReplicaSet-and-shift-traffic sequence. That sequence is the feature, not something to route around.
misconceptions.fact: A ReplicaSet has no update or versioning logic: editing its template only affects Pods it creates after the edit, and every already-running Pod is left untouched.

exercises.prompt: A Deployment has replicas=3, maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0, and is rolling from v1 to v2. At the single busiest moment of this rollout, what is the maximum possible total number of Pods (old + new combined), and what is the minimum number of Pods that must remain Available throughout the entire rollout?
exercises.code:
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
hints: maxSurge=1 caps how far ABOVE the desired count (3) the total is allowed to go at any instant.
maxUnavailable=0 caps how far BELOW the desired count the number of available Pods is allowed to drop -- what does a value of exactly 0 mean for that lower bound?
Work out the two bounds independently: one bounds the ceiling on total Pods, the other bounds the floor on available Pods.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Maximum total Pods at once: 4 (desired 3 + maxSurge 1). Minimum Available throughout: 3. maxUnavailable=0 means the available count is never allowed to drop even by one, so a new Pod must be confirmed Ready before any old Pod is removed, at every single step.
exercises.solutionExplanation: maxSurge=1 lets the controller create one extra Pod above the desired 3 before removing any old one, capping the total at 4 during the transition. maxUnavailable=0 is the stricter constraint: the number of available Pods may never fall below the desired 3, even briefly, so the controller can't delete an old Pod until a new one has been created and confirmed Ready, since deleting first would drop availability to 2. This combination (surge above, zero tolerance for unavailability) is a common choice for latency-sensitive services where even a few seconds of reduced capacity is unacceptable, at the cost of running one extra Pod's worth of resources at each step.

exercises.prompt: This Deployment's owner wanted a 'fast, aggressive rollout' for a latency-sensitive service. In practice, every rollout causes a brief but total outage -- all old Pods disappear before any new ones are confirmed ready. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 0%
      maxUnavailable: 100%
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.26
hints: maxUnavailable=100% means the controller is allowed to let the ENTIRE desired count become unavailable at once -- what does that let it do to the old Pods before any new one exists?
maxSurge=0% means the controller isn't allowed to create even a single extra Pod above the desired count before removing an old one -- so with unavailability also uncapped, what has to happen first?
Compare this configuration's effective behavior to the Recreate strategy discussed in this concept -- are they actually different in this specific case?
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.26
exercises.solutionExplanation: With maxSurge: 0% the controller can't create a new Pod before removing an old one (no room to surge above the desired count), and with maxUnavailable: 100% it may let every old Pod become unavailable at once. Together the only available sequence is: delete all old Pods, then create new ones. That's a full outage, equivalent to the Recreate strategy despite being configured as 'RollingUpdate.' The fix is a nonzero maxSurge (25%, the default, which is one extra Pod for 4 replicas) so new Pods are created and confirmed Ready before old ones are removed, plus maxUnavailable: 0 so the available count never drops below the desired total. Together they restore a zero-downtime rollout instead of the fast but outage-causing one that was configured. Kubernetes also rejects a strategy where both maxSurge and maxUnavailable are zero, since the rollout could then never make progress.

assessments.prompt: Midway through a rolling update, you run `kubectl get rs -l app=web` and see two ReplicaSets for the same Deployment, both showing a nonzero DESIRED and CURRENT count at the same time. What does this indicate?
options: This is expected, transient, in-flight state -- the Deployment controller is concurrently scaling the new ReplicaSet up and the old one down within the bounds set by maxSurge/maxUnavailable.
This is a bug -- a Deployment should only ever have exactly one ReplicaSet with a nonzero count at any given time, and seeing two indicates a stuck or broken rollout.
It means maxSurge and maxUnavailable were both misconfigured to allow more Pods than the Deployment's own replicas field specifies.
It means the cluster accidentally created two unrelated Deployments that happen to share the app=web label.
assessments.explanation: Two ReplicaSets with nonzero counts is what a rolling update in progress looks like: the Deployment controller creates (or reuses) a new ReplicaSet and shifts replicas from the old one to the new one gradually, bounded by maxSurge/maxUnavailable, so both have Pods running for the rollout's duration. The “This is a bug -- a Deployment…” option is wrong: this is normal, and would only warrant investigation if the rollout stays in this state well past when it should have finished (check kubectl rollout status and progressDeadlineSeconds). The “It means the cluster accidentally created two…” option misreads the label match as a coincidence, when it's the Deployment's own selector finding both of its ReplicaSets. The “It means maxSurge and maxUnavailable were both…” option confuses the transient total (which can briefly exceed desired replicas by up to maxSurge, by design) with a misconfiguration.

assessments.prompt: You directly edit a running ReplicaSet's `.spec.template` to change its container image, without touching the owning Deployment at all. What happens to the Pods currently running under that ReplicaSet?
options: The Deployment immediately detects the drift and reverts the ReplicaSet's template back to match its own .spec.template within seconds.
All existing Pods are immediately deleted and recreated with the new image, exactly as a Deployment-driven rollout would do.
None of the already-running Pods change at all -- the edit only affects Pods the ReplicaSet creates from that point forward.
The API server rejects the edit outright, since a ReplicaSet's template becomes immutable once any Pods matching its selector exist.
assessments.explanation: A ReplicaSet has no concept of 'update'. It ensures N Pods matching its selector exist and compares actual count against desired count, never an existing Pod's spec against the current template. Editing the template changes the Pods it creates from then on, and every Pod already running is left alone. The “All existing Pods are immediately deleted…” option describes Deployment-driven rolling-update behavior, which a bare ReplicaSet lacks. The “The API server rejects the edit outright…” option is false: Kubernetes doesn't lock a ReplicaSet's template once Pods exist. The “The Deployment immediately detects the drift…” option is false in the short term: the Deployment controller doesn't watch for this kind of direct edit and correct it on a timer, though a later Deployment-driven change would likely create yet another new ReplicaSet from the Deployment's own unedited template, sidelining the manual edit.

assessments.prompt: A CI pipeline runs `kubectl rollout status deployment/web` after applying a new image, wanting the pipeline to fail automatically if the rollout never actually completes rather than hanging forever. Which mechanism is actually responsible for that failure being surfaced?
options: kubectl rollout status polls indefinitely with no failure condition of its own; a separate, unrelated monitoring tool must always be configured to catch a stuck rollout.

The Deployment's progressDeadlineSeconds field (default 600s) causes the Deployment to surface a ProgressDeadlineExceeded condition once the rollout hasn't made forward progress within that window, and kubectl rollout status detects and reports that condition as a failure.
kubectl rollout status has a hardcoded 30-second timeout, after which it always exits with an error regardless of how the Deployment is configured.
The readinessProbe itself has a built-in global timeout that automatically fails the entire Deployment object after a fixed number of probe failures.
assessments.explanation: progressDeadlineSeconds is the field for this: if the rollout makes no progress within that window, the Deployment records a ProgressDeadlineExceeded status condition, and kubectl rollout status (which watches those conditions rather than applying a timeout of its own) reports the failure and exits nonzero, so a CI pipeline fails fast instead of hanging. The “kubectl rollout status has a hardcoded 30-second…” option invents a timeout that doesn't exist. The “The readinessProbe itself has a built-in global…” option misattributes deadline behavior to the readinessProbe, which reports one Pod's health, not the Deployment's rollout progress. The “kubectl rollout status polls indefinitely…” option is wrong: the mechanism is built into the Deployment object and kubectl, with no external tool required.

assessments.prompt: After a rolling update finishes, the old ReplicaSet (now scaled to 0 replicas) is not deleted immediately. Why is it retained, and what does that retention directly enable?
options: It's retained so the ReplicaSet controller can average resource-usage metrics across old and new ReplicaSets for autoscaling decisions.
It's retained purely so `kubectl get rs` output looks complete; it has no functional purpose and could be deleted immediately with zero effect on future operations.
It's retained because Kubernetes never deletes any object automatically under any circumstance; a human must manually run kubectl delete rs on every old ReplicaSet.

It's retained (up to revisionHistoryLimit) specifically so `kubectl rollout undo` can simply scale it back up while scaling the current ReplicaSet down -- reusing the existing object instead of rebuilding a new ReplicaSet and re-pulling images from scratch.
assessments.explanation: That is why rollbacks are fast: kubectl rollout undo doesn't rebuild anything, it re-triggers the scale-up/scale-down mechanism of a forward rollout, pointed at a previous ReplicaSet that already exists (as long as it's within revisionHistoryLimit). The “It's retained purely so `kubectl get rs`…” option understates the functional purpose. The “It's retained because Kubernetes never deletes any…” option is false: Kubernetes deletes plenty automatically (old ReplicaSets beyond revisionHistoryLimit are garbage collected); retention here is a bounded policy, not an inability to delete. The “It's retained so the ReplicaSet controller can…” option describes a capability the ReplicaSet controller doesn't have, since it has no autoscaling logic of its own.

assessments.prompt: Explain, layer by layer -- Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod -- exactly what gets created versus mutated at each layer when you change the container image in a Deployment's Pod template and Kubernetes performs a rolling update.
assessments.modelAnswer: At the Deployment layer, the object you edited is mutated in place: .spec.template.spec.containers[].image changes on the existing Deployment, and no new Deployment is created. The Deployment controller reacts by computing a hash of the new Pod template and checking whether a ReplicaSet with that hash exists. For a new image tag it doesn't, so a new ReplicaSet is created at the ReplicaSet layer, initially scaled to 0. The previous ReplicaSet (matching the old template hash) is left in place, untouched, still holding the full desired count for now. The Deployment controller then alternately raises the new ReplicaSet's replica count and lowers the old one's, bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable and waiting for new Pods to pass their readiness probe along the way. At the Pod layer, new Pod objects are created by the new ReplicaSet (new names, new IPs, running the new image) while old Pods, owned by the old ReplicaSet, are deleted as the new ones become Ready. No existing Pod is ever mutated or upgraded in place; every Pod running the new image is one that didn't exist before the rollout. Once the new ReplicaSet reaches the full desired count and the old one reaches zero, the rollout is complete, and the old ReplicaSet is retained (scaled to zero), up to revisionHistoryLimit, so that a later rollback can reuse it instead of building a new one.

concepts.title: Services: Stable Networking for Ephemeral Pods
concepts.description: Pods are disposable and their IPs churn, so Kubernetes needs a stable, load-balanced front door in front of a set of Pods that never stops changing: a Service. Understanding how that front door is implemented, via Endpoints/EndpointSlices and kube-proxy rewriting packets, turns 'it just works' networking into something you can debug.
learningObjectives: Explain the problem a Service solves, tying it directly to Pod IP churn covered in the Pods concept.
Explain how a Service finds the Pods that back it via label selectors, and where that resolved list is actually stored (Endpoints/EndpointSlice objects).
Explain, conceptually, how kube-proxy uses that list to get a packet from 'client sends to the Service's ClusterIP' to 'packet arrives at a specific Pod IP.'
Distinguish ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Service types and identify when each is appropriate.
Explain why a Pod that is Running but not yet Ready is excluded from a Service's routable endpoints, and why this matters for zero-downtime rollouts.
Debug a 'Service has no traffic reaching Pods' scenario by checking selector/label mismatches and inspecting whether Endpoints are populated.

sections.heading: The Problem: Pods Are a Moving Target
sections.body:
As covered in the Pods concept, a Pod's IP address is not durable: it changes every time the Pod is replaced, and during any rolling update, scaling event, or node failure several Pods with different IPs may appear and disappear in quick succession. Nothing that needs to reach 'the web app' can hardcode a Pod's IP; it would go stale within minutes, sometimes seconds.

A **Service** is Kubernetes' answer: a stable virtual IP address (its ClusterIP) and a stable DNS name, sitting in front of a changing set of Pods selected by label. Clients talk to the Service's stable address (inside the same namespace the short name `web` works; from elsewhere use `web.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`), and the Service (via mechanisms covered below) gets the traffic to whichever Pods currently back it, without the client needing to know how many there are or what their IPs are at that moment.

sections.heading: Selectors, Endpoints, and EndpointSlices
sections.body:
A Service finds its backing Pods using the same label-matching mechanism a ReplicaSet uses to find the Pods it owns:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```

A separate controller (the EndpointSlice controller) continuously watches for Pods matching that selector, paying attention to their **Ready** condition, and writes the current (IP, port) pairs to route to into `EndpointSlice` objects (older clusters and tooling use an `Endpoints` object for the same information; EndpointSlices are the more scalable representation). This is the mechanism behind 'traffic doesn't get sent to a Pod that isn't ready yet': only Pods passing their readiness probe are in this list. That is why a correct `readinessProbe` matters for a zero-downtime rollout, tying back to the rolling-update mechanics from the previous concept: a new Pod that's Running but not yet Ready is invisible to any Service pointed at it.

`kubectl get endpoints web` (or `kubectl get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web`) is the most useful command for debugging Service traffic, because it shows what the selector resolved to right now. Newer Kubernetes releases deprecate the Endpoints API in favor of EndpointSlice, and recent kubectl versions print a warning, but the command still works.

sections.heading: kube-proxy: How a Packet Gets From ClusterIP to a Pod
sections.body:
A Service's ClusterIP is **virtual**. It doesn't correspond to any network interface in the cluster, and nothing 'listens' on it the way a process listens on a socket. **kube-proxy**, running on every node, watches Services and their EndpointSlices and programs the node's packet-handling layer (historically iptables rules doing destination NAT; IPVS or nftables in some clusters, and eBPF-based replacements in others) so that any packet addressed to a Service's ClusterIP and port is rewritten in flight to target one of the currently Ready backing Pod IPs. The choice is effectively random per new connection, with no awareness of Pod load or health beyond Ready/not-Ready.

This rewriting happens in the kernel networking layer of the node the traffic originates from. The calling Pod never 'knows' it addressed a virtual IP that got rewritten; it opened a TCP connection to an address and got a response, as with any other IP. It's also why a plain kube-proxy-backed Service works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP): it has no notion of HTTP paths, headers, retries, or circuit breaking, because it rewrites packets and doesn't parse requests. Ingress controllers and service meshes fill that gap one layer up, which is out of scope here.

sections.heading: ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer
sections.body:
**ClusterIP** (the default type) is reachable only from inside the cluster, and is the normal choice for most Service-to-Service traffic, where nothing external needs to reach it.

**NodePort** builds on ClusterIP by also opening a fixed port (30000-32767 by default) on every node's IP, so external traffic can reach the Service by hitting *any* node's IP on that port. NodePort is usually a building block rather than a production end-state: callers need to know and track individual node IPs, and there's no single stable address to hand out.

**LoadBalancer**, on a cloud provider, allocates a NodePort as above *and* asks the cloud-controller-manager to provision a managed external load balancer that forwards to that NodePort across the cluster's nodes. So LoadBalancer is a superset of NodePort's mechanism, not a separate one. On a bare-metal cluster with no cloud-controller-manager implementation, a LoadBalancer Service's `.status.loadBalancer` stays pending forever unless something like MetalLB is installed to do that provisioning step.

A brief mention: a **headless Service** (`clusterIP: None`) skips the virtual IP and kube-proxy rewriting. DNS lookups for it return each backing Pod's IP, rather than one shared virtual address (several A records under the one Service name). It's used when clients need to address individual Pods by identity (StatefulSets are the canonical example), rather than 'any one of an interchangeable pool,' which is the assumption every other Service type is built around.

sections.heading: Debugging 'My Service Has No Traffic'
sections.body:
A checklist, roughly in the order to check things:

1. **`kubectl get endpoints <svc>`**: an empty address list is the most common symptom, and it means the selector matched zero Ready Pods. Check for a label mismatch between `Service.spec.selector` and the Pod template's labels first. Matching is exact and case-sensitive (`app: web` will not match `app: Web`), with no partial or fuzzy matching.
2. If Endpoints *are* populated but traffic still fails, check what the Pods are doing end to end. A Pod can be `Running` but not `Ready`, and is then correctly *excluded* from Endpoints. That's not a bug in the Service; it's the readinessProbe doing its job, and the fix is in the probe or the application.
3. Check for a `port` vs. `targetPort` mixup: `port` is what clients use to reach the Service; `targetPort` is the port the container listens on inside the Pod. `targetPort` defaults to the value of `port`, not to whatever the container listens on. A container listening on 8080 behind a Service that omits `targetPort: 8080` will get traffic on the wrong port, with no error from Kubernetes, even though the Pod is healthy and Ready.

examples.title: A Service and Deployment With Matching Labels
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.26
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
examples.explanation: The Service's selector (app: web) matches the label the Deployment stamps onto every Pod it creates (metadata.labels.app: web in the Pod template). That shared label is the only connection between these two objects; neither references the other by name. `kubectl get endpoints web` here shows three addresses, one per Ready Pod, each on port 8080 (the targetPort; the unprivileged nginx image listens on 8080), not port 80, which is only the port clients use to reach the Service. If a fourth, unrelated Pod in the same namespace also carried the label app: web, this Service would pick it up too, intended or not: selectors match on labels alone, with no awareness of which controller created the Pod.

examples.title: A Label Mismatch Producing Empty Endpoints
examples.code:
kubectl get svc web -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
# {"app":"web-app"}

kubectl get pods --show-labels
# NAME                  LABELS
# web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp    app=web
# web-7d9f8c9b7-9plm2    app=web
# web-7d9f8c9b7-k7q3z    app=web

kubectl get endpoints web
# NAME   ENDPOINTS   AGE
# web    <none>      4m
examples.explanation: The Service's selector is app=web-app, but every Pod is labeled app=web. A one-word difference, and since label matching is exact and case-sensitive, this Service matches nothing. The Endpoints object confirms it: <none>. This is the first thing to check when a Service seems to have Pods 'behind' it but traffic goes nowhere. Before suspecting kube-proxy, network policy, or firewalls, confirm the Endpoints object is populated, because if it's empty, kube-proxy has correctly programmed zero rewrite rules for this Service. Nothing is broken in the networking layer, only in the selector.

examples.title: LoadBalancer as NodePort Plus a Cloud-Provisioned Front Door
examples.code:
kubectl get svc web -o wide
# NAME   TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP      PORT(S)
# web    LoadBalancer   10.96.14.201   203.0.113.42     80:31842/TCP
examples.explanation: The PORT(S) column, 80:31842/TCP, shows the LoadBalancer/NodePort relationship: 80 is the port clients use against the external IP, and 31842 is the NodePort allocated on every node, as it would be for a plain NodePort Service. The cloud provider's load balancer, reachable at 203.0.113.42, forwards traffic to that same NodePort across the cluster's nodes. It's an extra layer in front of the NodePort mechanism, not a replacement. On a cluster with no cloud-controller-manager able to provision that load balancer (bare metal with nothing like MetalLB), EXTERNAL-IP would show <pending> indefinitely, while the NodePort (31842) would still work if you hit any node's IP directly on that port.

misconceptions.description: A Service is basically a load-balancer process or Pod running somewhere in the cluster that receives traffic and forwards it along, similar to how an nginx reverse proxy would work.
misconceptions.clarification: No such process exists. A Service's ClusterIP is a virtual address that no listening process on any host ever binds; kube-proxy implements routing by programming packet-rewriting (destination NAT) rules into the network stack of every node. A Service is closer to a distributed set of firewall/NAT rules, kept in sync across nodes, than to a running program. There is no single place you could kubectl exec into and find 'the load balancer' for a Service.

misconceptions.description: As soon as a new Pod's container status shows Running, a Service pointed at it will immediately start sending it traffic.
misconceptions.clarification: Running only means the container process has started. It says nothing about whether the application is ready to serve (it might still be loading a cache, connecting to a database, or running startup migrations). The EndpointSlice controller checks the Pod's Ready condition, driven by its readinessProbe, and only Ready Pods are added to the address list kube-proxy routes to. A Pod can sit in Running for a long time while correctly excluded from all Service traffic. And if no readinessProbe is configured, a Pod counts as Ready as soon as its containers are running, an easy-to-miss footgun for anything with a nontrivial startup sequence.

exercises.prompt: A Service has selector app=web. Four Pods exist: three are labeled app=web and are Ready; one is labeled app=web,tier=canary and is Running but currently failing its readiness probe. How many addresses will `kubectl get endpoints web` show, and which Pods are they?
exercises.code:
kubectl get pods --show-labels
# NAME    LABELS               READY
# pod-a   app=web              1/1
# pod-b   app=web              1/1
# pod-c   app=web              1/1
# pod-d   app=web,tier=canary  0/1
hints: Does the Service's selector care about the extra tier=canary label at all, or only about whether app=web is present and matches?
Endpoints are built from Pods matching the selector AND passing their readiness check -- both conditions have to hold, independently.
pod-d matches the label selector just fine. What specifically disqualifies it, and is that a Service-level decision or a Pod-level one?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 3 addresses: pod-a, pod-b, and pod-c. pod-d matches the selector (app=web is present, and a selector only requires the specified key(s) to match, ignoring any extra labels like tier=canary) but is excluded because it isn't Ready.
exercises.solutionExplanation: A label selector like app=web matches any Pod with that key-value pair, whatever other labels it carries, so pod-d's extra tier=canary label doesn't stop it matching. What excludes pod-d is separate: the EndpointSlice controller includes only Pods that both match the selector and are currently Ready, and pod-d shows 0/1, meaning it's failing its readiness check. So the Endpoints object has 3 addresses (pod-a, pod-b, pod-c), and pod-d, despite matching the selector, receives no traffic from this Service until its readiness probe passes.

exercises.prompt: A team deployed a Service and a Deployment together, but `kubectl get endpoints web` shows no addresses at all, even though `kubectl get pods` shows 3 healthy, Ready Pods. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: Web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.26
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
hints: Label matching is an exact string comparison -- compare the Service's selector value character by character against the Pod template's label value.
Case matters. 'Web' and 'web' are two completely different string values as far as a selector is concerned.
The fix is a one-character change, and it's in the Service, not the Deployment.
exercises.solutionCode:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.26
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
exercises.solutionExplanation: The Service's selector says app: Web (capital W), while every Pod from the Deployment carries app: web (lowercase). Label matching is an exact, case-sensitive string comparison, so the values are unequal and the Service matches zero Pods even though all three are healthy and Ready. Lowercasing the selector to app: web fixes it, and kubectl get endpoints web will list all three Pod addresses. This is the kind of bug the 'check Endpoints first, then the selector text' order from this concept catches quickly, instead of jumping to suspect kube-proxy or the network.

assessments.prompt: A Service is defined with `port: 80` and `targetPort: 8080`, backed by Pods running a container that listens on 8080. A client inside the cluster runs `curl http://web:80`. What actually happens at the networking level?
options: kube-proxy rewrites the destination of the outgoing packet from the Service's ClusterIP:80 to a specific backing Pod's IP:8080, chosen from the current Endpoints list.
Port 80 is rewritten to whatever port the Service itself happens to be listening on, which is always the same as the ClusterIP's own port.
The Pod's container must also be listening on port 80, or the connection is refused outright.
A dedicated Service Pod, running somewhere in the cluster, receives the connection on port 80 and manually proxies it to a backend Pod on port 8080.
assessments.explanation: This is what port and targetPort are for: port (80) is what the client addresses, and kube-proxy's rules rewrite the destination to a backing Pod's IP and targetPort (8080) as the packet passes through the node's network stack. It's a Layer 4 rewrite with no proxying process involved. The “The Pod's container must also be listening…” option misunderstands targetPort, which exists to decouple the Service's port from the port the container listens on. The “A dedicated Service Pod, running somewhere…” option is false: no standalone Service process exists, and the rewriting happens in the node's kernel networking layer, not in a proxy Pod. The “Port 80 is rewritten to whatever port…” option is nonsensical: a ClusterIP doesn't 'listen' on anything, being purely virtual.

assessments.prompt: A StatefulSet's Pods need to be addressed individually by identity (pod-0, pod-1, ...) rather than through one shared virtual IP that could route to any interchangeable backend. Which Service configuration supports this, and what does it change about DNS resolution?
options: A standard ClusterIP Service -- DNS resolution behaves identically to any other Service, since kube-proxy always resolves individual Pod identities transparently underneath the shared virtual IP.
A NodePort Service -- NodePort's fixed port-per-node model is specifically what lets clients address individual Pods instead of a virtual IP.
A headless Service (clusterIP: None) -- it skips the virtual IP and kube-proxy packet rewriting entirely, so DNS lookups for the Service return each individual backing Pod's IP directly.
No Service configuration supports this; StatefulSet Pods must always be addressed by hardcoding their current Pod IPs directly.
assessments.explanation: A headless Service is the mechanism for this case: with clusterIP: None there's no virtual IP and no kube-proxy rewriting, so a DNS lookup against the Service name returns the individual IPs of the matching Ready Pods, letting a client (or a StatefulSet Pod's stable per-Pod DNS name) address one Pod by identity instead of an interchangeable pool. The “A standard ClusterIP Service -- DNS resolution…” option is false: a normal ClusterIP Service hides individual Pod identity behind one shared virtual address, the opposite of what's needed. The “A NodePort Service -- NodePort's fixed port-per-node…” option credits NodePort with something it doesn't do; NodePort is ClusterIP plus a node-level port and has nothing to do with per-Pod addressing. The “No Service configuration supports this; StatefulSet Pods…” option is false: hardcoding Pod IPs is the fragile anti-pattern Services exist to avoid, and a headless Service meets the identity requirement without it.

assessments.prompt: A container listens on port 9000. The Service manifest sets `port: 9000` and omits `targetPort` entirely. `kubectl get endpoints` shows all Pods correctly listed, yet requests through the Service still fail. Is the missing `targetPort` field the cause?
options: Yes -- an omitted targetPort silently defaults to port 80 regardless of what port is set to, so traffic is being routed to port 80 on Pods that aren't listening there.
No -- targetPort has no effect on routing whatsoever; it is purely a documentation field with no bearing on how kube-proxy rewrites packets.
Yes -- targetPort must always be explicitly set, or the Service is invalid and would never populate Endpoints at all.
No -- when targetPort is omitted, it defaults to the same value as port (9000), which matches the container's actual listening port here.
assessments.explanation: This tests the defaulting rule: when targetPort is unset, Kubernetes defaults it to the value of port, not to some fixed value, and the Service is still valid. Since port is 9000 and the container listens on 9000, the effective targetPort already matches, so this configuration is not the bug; the failure must come from something else (a NetworkPolicy blocking traffic, an application-level error, a firewall). Jumping to 'must be a port mismatch' without checking the values leads to the wrong fix: the debugging checklist is meant to be followed by reading the numbers, not applied as a reflex.

assessments.prompt: A team wants a Service to route requests based on the HTTP request path -- for example, `/api` to one set of Pods and `/static` to another -- without adding any component beyond a plain ClusterIP Service. Why can't kube-proxy alone do this?
options: kube-proxy does inspect HTTP paths by default, but only when the Service type is LoadBalancer rather than ClusterIP.

kube-proxy operates purely at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), rewriting packet destinations without ever parsing an HTTP request -- it has no concept of paths, headers, or any other Layer 7 detail, so path-based routing requires a separate component (an Ingress controller or service mesh) operating one layer up.
A single Service object actually can map different targetPort values to different URL paths; the team just hasn't discovered that field of the Service spec yet.
This is only a limitation on bare-metal clusters; any cloud-managed cluster's kube-proxy automatically gains Layer 7 path-based routing for free.
assessments.explanation: kube-proxy rewrites a packet's destination IP and port based on Endpoints. It has no visibility into the payload of the TCP stream, so it cannot route on something as high-level as an HTTP path, which lives well above Layer 4. That gap is what Ingress controllers or a service mesh fill, not any hidden Service field. None of the other options describe real capabilities: there's no per-path targetPort mapping on a Service, no LoadBalancer-specific HTTP awareness in kube-proxy, and no cloud-specific exception to the Layer 4 boundary.

assessments.prompt: Explain the full path a request takes from a client Pod calling a Service's DNS name to a response coming back from a specific backing Pod, and explain specifically what being listed in a Service's Endpoints does -- and does not -- guarantee about that Pod's ability to actually handle the request correctly.
assessments.modelAnswer: When a client Pod resolves the Service's DNS name, it gets the Service's stable ClusterIP, a virtual address with no listener anywhere. When the client opens a connection to that ClusterIP on the Service's port, the packet passes through the network stack of the node the client Pod runs on, where kube-proxy has already programmed destination-NAT rules (based on the Service's current EndpointSlices) that rewrite the destination to one backing Pod's IP and targetPort, chosen effectively at random among the eligible backends for that new connection. From there the packet is routed through the cluster network to that Pod, which responds as if it had received an ordinary connection; the client never sees the rewriting. Being listed in Endpoints guarantees two things: the Pod matched the Service's label selector, and its Ready condition was true the last time the endpoints controller checked. It does NOT guarantee the request about to be sent will succeed. The Pod could still fail this request for reasons unrelated to its aggregate Ready status (a transient error, a flaky dependency, a bug that shows up on certain inputs), and kube-proxy has no request-level awareness, since it works at Layer 4 and commits to a destination before any application-level response exists. Endpoints membership is a coarse, point-in-time signal of routing eligibility, not a per-request success guarantee. Retries, circuit breaking, and request-aware load balancing have to come from a service mesh or an application-level client library.

concepts.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets: Externalizing Configuration
concepts.description: Baking environment-specific configuration or credentials into a container image defeats the point of building one image and promoting it unchanged across environments. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject that configuration at runtime instead. Knowing how and when injection happens (env vars vs. mounted files) and what a 'Secret' does and doesn't protect against prevents some dangerous assumptions.
learningObjectives: Explain why configuration should be externalized from container images, and how ConfigMaps/Secrets achieve that.
Consume a ConfigMap both as environment variables and as a mounted volume, and explain the practical difference between the two, especially around updates.
Explain what a Secret actually is under the hood, and precisely what protection it does and does not provide compared to a plain ConfigMap.
Predict whether a running Pod picks up a change to a ConfigMap or Secret it's already using, for both the env-var and mounted-volume consumption styles.
Explain why committing a rendered Secret manifest (plain YAML containing a base64-encoded value) to a git repository is a real credential leak, not a safe practice.

sections.heading: Why Externalize Configuration At All
sections.body:
The argument is the same one behind twelve-factor-style configuration: build a single, tested, immutable image and promote that *same artifact* through dev, staging, and production. If a database connection string or a feature flag were baked in at build time, you'd need a separate image build per environment, which defeats the idea of an artifact tested once and trusted everywhere. A configuration change (rotating an endpoint, tweaking a timeout) also shouldn't require a rebuild-push-redeploy cycle to take effect.

A **ConfigMap** holds non-sensitive key-value data (URLs, feature flags, whole config files), decoupled from both the container image and the Pod spec that references it. A **Secret** is structurally almost identical to a ConfigMap and is intended for sensitive data: passwords, tokens, certificates. 'Intended for' carries weight here, and a later section covers why: the intention doesn't come with strong protection attached.

sections.heading: Consuming a ConfigMap: Environment Variables vs. Mounted Files
sections.body:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: web-config
data:
  DATABASE_URL: "postgres://db:5432/app"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
```

Consumed as an environment variable (via `envFrom` or a per-key `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef`), the value is read **once**, at container start, and put into that process's environment by the container runtime. If the ConfigMap changes afterward, a running container never sees the new value. Environment variables have no live-update mechanism; the only way a running Pod picks up a changed value consumed this way is for the Pod to be replaced. `kubectl rollout restart deployment/web` does exactly that, as a normal rolling replacement, without editing the Deployment.

Consumed instead as a **mounted volume**, the files inside the Pod are synced by the kubelet to the ConfigMap's current contents (on the order of a minute, subject to the kubelet's sync period, not instantly) *without* restarting the Pod. This only helps if the application notices the file changed on disk (via inotify, or by re-reading it periodically). Kubernetes updates the file; it doesn't make the application re-read it, and most applications read a config file once at startup and never again. One more catch: a ConfigMap mounted with `subPath` is never updated in the running container.

The practical guidance: for anything you want a running Pod to pick up without a restart, use a mounted file *and* make sure the application watches it. For configuration that can wait for the next deploy or restart, which is most of it, environment variables are simpler and need no application-side logic. For ConfigMaps and Secrets that should never change under a running Pod, `immutable: true` makes the object read-only after creation, which also reduces load on the API server.

sections.heading: What a Secret Is (and Isn't)
sections.body:
A Secret's values are stored **base64-encoded**, not encrypted. Base64 is an encoding, not a cipher: it has no key, and anyone with read access to the Secret object (or a copy of its rendered YAML) can decode it with `echo <value> | base64 -d`. This needs stating bluntly because the misconception is common and dangerous.

The protection that does exist, layer by layer:

1. **etcd encryption at rest**, only if the cluster operator has configured an `EncryptionConfiguration` for the API server. This is not on by default in many clusters.
2. **RBAC**, restricting which users and service accounts may `get`/`list` Secret objects. This is the access-control boundary that matters day to day, not the base64 encoding.
3. The kubelet mounts Secrets into Pods via `tmpfs` (RAM-backed storage) instead of writing them to the node's persistent disk, which reduces, though doesn't eliminate, the risk of credentials lingering on a node's disk after a Pod is gone.

Put plainly: a Secret is 'a ConfigMap with a naming convention, plus a few default handling niceties (tmpfs mounts, kubectl not printing values in some views) that signal *treat this as sensitive*.' It is not a vault and not encrypted by default. (A Secret manifest can use `stringData` to carry plaintext values that the API server encodes into `data` when it stores them, but reading the object back always shows base64.) For rotation, audit trails, dynamic short-lived credentials, and strong encryption guarantees, production clusters typically integrate an external secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, a cloud provider's KMS-backed secret store) rather than relying on core Secret objects alone.

sections.heading: The Git Leak Footgun
sections.body:
```bash
kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
  --from-literal=password=hunter2 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml
# apiVersion: v1
# kind: Secret
# data:
#   password: aHVudGVyMg==
```

That `aHVudGVyMg==` is base64 for `hunter2`: one trivial command from plaintext for anyone who can read the file's text, with no cluster access needed. Committing a rendered Secret manifest like this to git, even a *private* repository, and certainly a public one, is the same as committing the plaintext password with a thin disguise. Git history keeps it forever, even after a later commit 'removes' the file, unless the history is rewritten and force-pushed (and existing clones or forks may still have it regardless).

The correct pattern is never to commit a rendered Secret manifest containing a real value. Either generate the Secret at deploy time from a secret store or a CI-injected environment variable and apply it without writing the real value to a file that touches version control, or use a tool built for this problem: Sealed Secrets and SOPS keep only an *encrypted* form in git, and the External Secrets Operator keeps only a reference to a secret stored elsewhere. In each case the real Secret object is created inside the cluster.

examples.title: The Same ConfigMap, Consumed Two Ways
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: web-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: my-app:1.0
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: web-config
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config-volume
              mountPath: /etc/app-config
      volumes:
        - name: config-volume
          configMap:
            name: web-config
examples.explanation: The same ConfigMap is wired in two ways here, and they behave differently after it changes. The envFrom entry injects LOG_LEVEL=info as an environment variable, resolved once when the container starts; if web-config is updated later, the running container's variable stays stale until the Pod is replaced. The volumeMount exposes the ConfigMap's keys as files under /etc/app-config (a file named LOG_LEVEL containing info) that the kubelet updates on disk within roughly a minute of the change. But only application code that watches that path will notice and react; nothing forces a re-read, and most applications never look at a config file again after reading it at startup.

examples.title: A Secret Is a Base64 Round Trip, Not Encryption
examples.code:
kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
  --from-literal=password=hunter2 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml
# apiVersion: v1
# kind: Secret
# metadata:
#   name: db-creds
# data:
#   password: aHVudGVyMg==

echo aHVudGVyMg== | base64 -d
# hunter2
examples.explanation: This is a two-command, zero-privilege round trip: anyone who can read the manifest's text, with no cluster access, no kubectl, and no RBAC permissions, can recover the password in seconds. Treating a checked-in Secret manifest as 'safe because it's not plaintext' is a false sense of security; the encoding gives no confidentiality on its own. The protections that matter are about who can read the object or the file in the first place: RBAC for the live cluster object, repository access controls for a file in git. The base64 wrapper contributes nothing.

misconceptions.description: Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted, so storing sensitive values there is inherently more secure than putting the same value in a ConfigMap, with no other precautions needed.
misconceptions.clarification: Base64 is not encryption. Unless a cluster operator has configured etcd encryption at rest, Secret data sits in etcd, and travels over the API, in a trivially reversible encoding: anyone who can run kubectl get secret -o yaml gets the real value back with one decode step. The security boundary is RBAC (who can read the Secret object at all), optionally combined with etcd encryption at rest and, for sensitive production credentials, an external secrets manager. It is not the base64 wrapper Secrets use, which ConfigMaps could just as easily have used.

misconceptions.description: Updating a ConfigMap that a running Deployment already references will immediately update the live application's configuration, the same way updating the Deployment's image field triggers a rolling update.
misconceptions.clarification: Whether and how fast a running Pod picks up a ConfigMap change depends on how it's consumed, and in neither case does Kubernetes push the new value into the running process. Environment-variable consumption is resolved once, at container start, and a running container never sees a ConfigMap update until its Pod is replaced by some other event (a new rollout, a manual restart). Mounted-volume consumption is updated on disk by the kubelet within roughly a minute, but it changes application behavior only if the application notices the file changed and re-reads it. Unlike an image change, a ConfigMap change never triggers a rollout or Pod restart by itself, for either consumption style.
misconceptions.fact: Whether and how fast a running Pod picks up a ConfigMap change depends entirely on how it's consumed, and in neither case does Kubernetes push the new value into the running process for you.

exercises.prompt: A Deployment's Pods consume a ConfigMap via envFrom. You update the ConfigMap with `kubectl apply`, without touching the Deployment or any Pod. Immediately afterward, you run `kubectl exec <pod> -- printenv LOG_LEVEL` against a Pod that was already running before the update. Does it show the old value or the new value, and why?
exercises.code:
kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml   # LOG_LEVEL changed from "info" to "debug"
kubectl exec web-7d9f8c9b7-4x2lp -- printenv LOG_LEVEL   # ?
hints: When exactly does Kubernetes resolve a configMapKeyRef or envFrom reference into an actual value inside a container's environment -- once, or continuously?
The container process that's already running was started before this ConfigMap update happened at all.
Is there any mechanism at all that pushes an updated environment variable value into an already-running process? Compare this to how the mounted-volume consumption style behaves.
exercises.expectedAnswer: It still shows the OLD value, "info". Environment variables sourced from a ConfigMap are resolved once, at container start, and baked into that process's environment block: there is no live mechanism that updates an already-running process's environment. Only a new Pod, created after the ConfigMap change, would show "debug".
exercises.solutionExplanation: envFrom (and configMapKeyRef) resolve their values once, when the container process starts, and the values go into that process's environment block via the container runtime; there is no ongoing connection back to the ConfigMap object. Updating the ConfigMap changes the object in etcd but doesn't reach into a running container and rewrite its environment; environment variables can't do that. The Pod queried here started before the update, so printenv reports the stale value, "info", and keeps doing so unless that Pod is deleted and replaced by a fresh one, which would resolve envFrom at its own startup and pick up "debug".

exercises.prompt: A security review flagged this deploy script as leaking a database credential, even though it only ever creates a Kubernetes 'Secret,' never a plain ConfigMap. The script's author argues this is fine because Secrets are encrypted. Identify what's actually wrong with the workflow and fix it.
exercises.code:
#!/bin/bash
kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
  --from-literal=password=SuperSecret123 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > secret.yaml
git add secret.yaml
git commit -m "Add db credentials"
hints: The kind of object being created (Secret vs ConfigMap) doesn't change what's happening to secret.yaml on disk -- what does that file actually contain, in a form anyone reading the repo could reverse?
The literal password is being written into a real file, and that file is then committed to git -- would that be a problem even if this were creating a ConfigMap instead of a Secret?
Fix the flow so the real value never gets written into a file that touches version control at all -- where should the real password actually come from at deploy time?
exercises.solutionCode:
#!/bin/bash
# The real password comes from CI's own secret store at deploy time,
# and is piped straight into apply: it never touches a file, let alone git.
kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
  --from-literal=password="$DB_PASSWORD" \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original script's bug has nothing to do with 'Secret vs ConfigMap.' The real password is written into a plain YAML file (secret.yaml) holding only a base64 encoding of it, and that file is committed to git, where anyone with repository access can recover it with one base64 -d, and where it stays recoverable in history even after later deletion. The fix removes both problems: DB_PASSWORD is read from an environment variable injected by the CI system's secret store at deploy time (never hardcoded or committed), and the rendered manifest is piped into kubectl apply -f - instead of being written to a file, let alone added to git. The author's 'Secrets are encrypted' defense is the misconception this concept warns about: base64 provides no confidentiality, so committing a rendered Secret manifest is as dangerous as committing the plaintext value.

assessments.prompt: What is the most accurate description of the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret in a vanilla Kubernetes cluster, with no additional tooling installed?
options: They are structurally almost identical -- both are key-value objects consumable as environment variables or mounted files.
ConfigMaps can only be consumed as environment variables, while Secrets can only be consumed as mounted files.
Secrets are strongly encrypted at rest by default, while ConfigMaps are never encrypted at all.
Secrets are stored in a separate, access-controlled datastore entirely apart from etcd, while ConfigMaps are stored in etcd.
assessments.explanation: A Secret and a ConfigMap share the same object shape and the same two consumption styles; the difference is a set of conventions (base64 encoding, kubectl's default display behavior) that signal intent rather than provide strong protection. The “Secrets are strongly encrypted at rest…” option overclaims: etcd encryption at rest for Secrets is an opt-in cluster configuration, not a default. The “ConfigMaps can only be consumed as environment…” option is false in both directions: both support env-var and mounted-file consumption. The “Secrets are stored in a separate, access-controlled…” option is false: Secrets live in etcd like every other Kubernetes object, with no separate datastore by default.

assessments.prompt: In a freshly installed Kubernetes cluster with no additional configuration applied, which of the following actually restricts who can read the plaintext value of a Secret?
options: etcd encryption at rest, which is enabled by default on every Kubernetes distribution out of the box.
Nothing at all by default -- Kubernetes intentionally ships with zero access control on Secret objects until an external secrets manager is installed.
RBAC rules controlling which users and ServiceAccounts are permitted to get/list Secret objects through the API server.
The base64 encoding itself, which functions as a lightweight cipher requiring a decode key that only cluster administrators possess.
assessments.explanation: RBAC is the access-control layer in effect out of the box, gating who can issue a get/list request against Secret objects through the API server. That's the day-to-day boundary. etcd encryption at rest is a valuable extra layer, but it's opt-in and off by default in many clusters, so the “etcd encryption at rest, which is enabled…” option overclaims. The “The base64 encoding itself, which functions…” option is false: base64 has no key and provides no confidentiality. The “Nothing at all by default -- Kubernetes…” option overstates the gap: RBAC is enforced by default (clusters typically ship with some default bindings), and just needs to be configured narrowly to be effective, which is different from having no access control.

assessments.prompt: An application mounts a ConfigMap as a volume and is written to read its config file only once, at process startup, with no file-watching logic at all. The ConfigMap is then updated via `kubectl apply`. What happens to the file on disk inside the already-running Pod, and does the application's behavior change?
options: Neither the file nor the application's behavior changes until the Pod itself is deleted and replaced, exactly like environment-variable consumption.
The file updates immediately, and the kubelet automatically sends a SIGHUP to the container's main process to force it to reload its configuration.
The mounted file is read-only and immutable for the entire lifetime of the Pod, so the ConfigMap update has no effect on it at all, ever.
The file on disk is updated by the kubelet within roughly a minute, but the application's behavior does not change.
assessments.explanation: Mounted-volume and environment-variable consumption differ at the file-system layer but not in forcing application behavior. The kubelet syncs the file on disk to the ConfigMap's current contents within roughly its sync period (about a minute), whether or not any application looks at it again. But Kubernetes can't force an application to re-read a file; that takes a watch (inotify) or periodic re-read in the application, which this one lacks. So the file changes but observable behavior doesn't, until a restart or new deploy makes the process re-read it. The “Neither the file nor the application's behavior…” option is wrong because it conflates mounted-volume behavior with env-var behavior: the file does update on disk, unlike an environment variable. The “The file updates immediately, and the kubelet…” and “The mounted file is read-only and immutable…” options describe mechanisms Kubernetes doesn't implement.

assessments.prompt: A team accidentally committed a rendered Secret manifest containing a real, live password to a git repository. They then deleted the file in a later commit and added it to .gitignore going forward. Is the credential now safe?
options: Yes, but only because the repository is private -- git history is only ever readable by the public in open-source repositories.

No -- the credential remains fully recoverable from the repository's git history (and any existing clones or forks) even after the file is deleted in a subsequent commit; deleting and gitignoring only prevents future commits from re-adding it, and the exposed credential should be treated as compromised and rotated.
Yes -- once a file is deleted in a later commit and gitignored, its contents are permanently purged from the repository and can no longer be recovered by anyone.
No, but only temporarily -- .gitignore actively scans and redacts the contents of past commits containing the same filename over time.
assessments.explanation: Deleting a file in a later commit doesn't erase it from git history: the object exists in every earlier commit reachable from the branch, and anyone with repository access (or a clone or fork made before the deletion) can check out an earlier commit and recover the file, real credential included. .gitignore only prevents that path from being added or tracked going forward; it has no retroactive effect and doesn't scan or redact past commits. The remedies are rewriting history (rebasing it out and force-pushing, which doesn't help against clones or forks that already have it) and, far more reliably, treating the credential as compromised and rotating it, as this concept's git-leak guidance recommends.

assessments.prompt: A teammate just discovered that `kubectl get secret db-creds -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d` reveals a plaintext password, and is alarmed, assuming this must be a bug. Explain why this is actually expected behavior, not a bug, and describe what genuinely prevents an unauthorized person from doing the exact same thing in a properly configured cluster.
assessments.modelAnswer: This is expected because a Secret's data field has only ever been base64-encoded, not encrypted. Base64 is a reversible encoding with no key, designed so arbitrary binary data can be carried inside a YAML/JSON text field, not to provide confidentiality. Decoding it with `base64 -d` is not a security flaw being exploited; it reverses an encoding that was always meant to be reversible. What stands between an unauthorized person and that plaintext, in a properly configured cluster, is mostly RBAC: the Kubernetes API enforces who may issue a `get` or `list` against Secret objects, and a well-configured cluster grants that narrowly, typically only to the ServiceAccounts and people who need it, following least privilege, instead of to every authenticated user. Beyond RBAC, an operator can configure etcd encryption at rest (via an EncryptionConfiguration on the API server), which protects the value if someone reaches etcd's storage or backups directly, bypassing the API server's RBAC checks. For high-value credentials, many teams go further and don't treat core Secret objects as the source of truth, integrating an external secrets manager such as Vault or a cloud KMS-backed store, which adds encryption, automatic rotation, and audit logging that a raw Secret was never designed to provide.
